title: Timber selection, treatment and fixings
audience: Deck and fence maintenance workers who select timber, treatment and fixings
learningOutcomes: Select timber and treatment suited to the exposure, the use and the manufacturer data.
Select fixings that suit the timber, the treatment and the load.
Identify the risk of mixing incompatible metals and treatments.

instruction.heading: Match the timber to the exposure
instruction.body: A timber deck or fence is chosen for the conditions it will meet, not for its appearance. Before a board, post or rail is selected, record where it will sit and what it will meet. Ground contact, rain, standing water, sun and the timber's position relative to the ground are all part of that record. Treated timber is labelled with a treatment class, and the class tells you the conditions it is intended for. The Queensland government guidance describes H1 to H3 as classes for timber kept off the ground, with H3 for timber exposed to weather or periodic wetting. It describes H4 as the class for timber in contact with the ground or continually damp, and H5 for timber in contact with the ground or fresh water. The same guidance says each class suits the conditions described for the lower classes as well. The practical rule is simple: a post in the ground needs a ground-contact class, and a rail above the ground needs a class for above-ground exposure. Use the class on the supplier's label and data sheet for the product you are actually buying, not the class you expect.

instruction.heading: Read the supplier data and keep the reference
instruction.body: Each product has its own supplier data. The data names the treatment class, the intended use and sometimes the species and grade. Read it before purchase, and record the product name, the grade, the treatment class and the date of the data sheet on the job record. If the supplier data does not name the class, or names a class that does not match the use, do not use the product for that use. Do not assume that because a timber is treated it is suitable for every use. A treated product in the wrong class can look sound for years and then fail at its base, so the record matters as much as the choice. Where the supplier does not give treatment instructions for cut ends or drilled holes, record that the instruction was not available and refer it, rather than inventing a method.

instruction.heading: Cut ends, holes and field treatment
instruction.body: Cutting and drilling exposes untreated timber. The Australian standard for timber preservation (AS 1604) is the usual reference for this work, but its text was not read in this pass, so its requirements are not stated here. Use the supplier's written instruction for field treatment where one is given, and record the product used and the area treated. Do not use an unlabelled or decanted preservative. Dust from cutting treated timber is also a hazard. Use dust control and the dust protection named in the product label or safety data sheet, and, as a working practice rather than a verified rule, avoid sweeping the dust up dry in an enclosed space.

instruction.heading: Fixings and compatibility
instruction.body: A fixing has to suit the timber, the treatment and the load. Some treatments corrode standard steel fixings, and some metals react when they are in contact with each other. Use fixings whose rating or coating is stated, in the supplier or manufacturer data, as suitable for the treatment and the exposure. Do not assume that a galvanised, stainless or coated fixing is suitable for every treatment. Pre-drill near the ends of boards to reduce splitting. Where a connection carries load into the structure, such as a post to a bearer or a handrail to a post, the fixing must be rated for the load and fixed into the structure. A surface screw through a deck board does not make a structural connection, and it should not be relied on for one. Corrosion and incompatibility often show up years after the work, which is why the fixing record matters.

instruction.heading: Handling and chemical safety
instruction.body: Preservatives, stains and other products used on timber are hazardous chemicals, and the safety data sheet for each product is the starting point for their use. Keep a current copy where workers can reach it, and make sure the people using the product can see it. Store products apart from any chemical they are incompatible with, and keep containers suited to the product, as the Safe Work Australia storage guidance describes. Do not decant products into unlabelled containers.

procedure: Record the exposure, the intended use and the load for each timber component, including whether it is in ground contact.
Select timber with a treatment class suited to that exposure, reading the product's supplier data for the class.
Record the product name, grade, treatment class and the date of the supplier data on the material record.
Select fixings whose rating or coating is stated for the treatment and the exposure, and check the manufacturer data for each metal pairing.
Pre-drill near ends and fix structural connections into the structure, using fixings rated for the load.
Treat cut ends and holes only with the method the supplier gives. Where no method is given, record that and refer it.
Check that each product on site has a current safety data sheet and is stored apart from any incompatible product.
Record the fixings and treatments used, with the supplier data reference, before the job is closed.

workedExamples.situation: A fence post is to be set in the ground. The supplier offers a timber whose label names only above-ground use. This is an example job.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should this timber be used for the post?
workedExamples.reasoning: No. The post is in ground contact, and the guidance describes ground contact as the class for H4 or H5. A product labelled for above-ground use is not the right class for this use. Choose a timber whose supplier data names a ground-contact class, record the product and its data reference, and do not use the above-ground product for the post.

workedExamples.situation: A deck board near a pool area needs replacing. The old board was fixed with steel screws that have corroded. This is an example job.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What fixing do you choose, and how do you check it?
workedExamples.reasoning: Choose a fixing whose manufacturer data names it as suitable for the treatment of the new board and for the exposure. Pre-drill near the board ends, and record the fixing product and the data reference. Do not reuse corroded screws, and do not assume the old fixing type is still the right choice.

workedExamples.situation: A handrail post on a deck needs to carry a handrail load. The plan is to fix the post with a surface screw through a deck board.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Is a surface screw an acceptable fixing for this connection?
workedExamples.reasoning: No. The post carries load, so the connection must be fixed into the structure with a fixing rated for the load. A surface screw through a board is not a structural connection. Stop the fixing, refer the connection to the designer or the approving authority, and record the referral. The design of structural connections is outside a maintenance worker's authority.

equipmentAndPpe: Supplier data sheet for each timber and treatment product, with the data reference recorded
Fixings with a stated rating or coating for the treatment and exposure, plus the manufacturer data
Pre-drill bits, drill and eye protection for drilling and cutting
Dust mask or respirator suited to the dust, as named on the product label or safety data sheet
Gloves suited to the product, as named on the label or safety data sheet

commonErrors.error: Using an above-ground treatment in ground contact.
commonErrors.prevention: Match the treatment class to the exposure using the supplier data, and check the class on the label.

commonErrors.error: Using standard steel fixings with a treatment that corrodes them.
commonErrors.prevention: Use fixings whose manufacturer data states suitability for the treatment, and check each metal pairing.

commonErrors.error: Making a structural connection with a surface fixing.
commonErrors.prevention: Fix load-carrying connections into the structure with fixings rated for the load, and refer the design.

commonErrors.error: Leaving the treatment and fixing choices unrecorded.
commonErrors.prevention: Write the product, grade, treatment class, fixing and data reference on the job record before the job is closed.

commonErrors.error: Cutting treated timber in a closed space without dust control.
commonErrors.prevention: Use dust control and the protection named on the label or safety data sheet, and do not sweep dust dry indoors.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Treatment classes: the Queensland government guidance says which classes suit above-ground exposure and which suit ground contact, and the selection rule in this lesson follows it. The guidance was last updated on 9 April 2020. Check the current supplier data for the product.
The Australian standard for timber preservation (AS 1604) was listed but its text was not read in this pass.
Chemical handling: keep a current safety data sheet for each product and make it easy to reach for everyone who uses or stores it. Store incompatible products well apart.

Selecting timber and fixings is a good-practice control. It does not give a carpentry licence, and it does not give authority to design or certify structural work. Structural decisions are covered by the permit and licence positions in “Deck and fence scope, permits and boundary survey” and “Footings, post setting and levels”.

qualityStandard: The treatment class of each timber matches the exposure, and the supplier data reference is recorded.
Fixings are rated for the treatment and the exposure, and the metal pairings are checked against the manufacturer data.
Load-carrying connections are fixed into the structure with fixings rated for the load, and no structural connection relies on a surface fixing.
Cut ends and holes are treated only as the supplier instructs, or the gap is recorded and referred.
documentationEvidence: Material record with product name, grade, treatment class, supplier data reference and date
Fixing record with the product, rating, coating and the manufacturer data reference
Record of any field treatment or referral for cut ends and holes
Confirmation that a current safety data sheet is on site for each chemical product used
summary: Match the treatment class to the exposure, and a timber in ground contact needs a ground-contact class.
Use fixings whose data states suitability for the treatment, and check each metal pairing.
Fix structural connections into the structure, and refer any design question.
Keep a current safety data sheet for each product, and record the materials and fixings used.

knowledgeChecks.question: A post is to be set in the ground. Which timber is correct?
options: Any treated timber, because all treated timber is the same
Untreated timber, because it is cheaper and easy to cut to length
Timber whose supplier data names a treatment class for ground contact
Timber whose label names above-ground use only, so it is cheaper

knowledgeChecks.question: Why must fixings be matched to the treatment?
options: Only for appearance, so the joint looks neat and matches the deck
Fixings do not interact with treatments, so any fixing will do
Some treatments corrode standard fixings, and the joint can fail later
The supplier decides the fixing, so the worker does not need to check

knowledgeChecks.question: A handrail post must carry a handrail load. Which connection is correct?
options: A surface screw through a deck board and into the joist below, since it holds the rail
A fixing rated for the load and fixed into the structure, as the design requires
Whatever fixing is in the toolbox that day, as long as it is strong enough to hold
Adhesive only, with no mechanical fixing, since the glue holds the rail firmly in place
